- If sentiment is strongly positive (≥0.7) and forecast is rising steadily, reduce forecast slope to avoid over-optimism.  
- If sentiment is strongly negative (≤-0.3) and forecast is falling, avoid excessive downward bias — consider slight upward correction.  
- When true outcome spikes sharply after a low, model often underreacts — adjust forecast to anticipate early momentum.  
- If recent history shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 days of consolidation), model should not overextend trend — cap forecast range within 1–2σ of recent mean.  
- Overshoot after a spike (forecast > true outcome by >5%) often occurs when sentiment is high — apply “cool-down” rule: reduce forecast by 1–2% per day after spike.  
- If sentiment is neutral or volatile (±0.2–0.5) and forecast is trending, check for lag — true outcome often moves 1–2 days ahead — adjust forecast to align with 1–2-day lag.  
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if sentiment is consistently positive, avoid linear extrapolation — introduce diminishing returns or exponential decay in forecast growth.  
- If true outcome is consistently below forecast (e.g., 3+ consecutive days), consider sentiment-driven “reversion bias” — reduce forecast by 0.5–1.5% per day until sentiment stabilizes.
